transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-14
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 54 minutes
Meeting ID: ml-20260914-001
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Elaine (Mariner Head of ML), Ben (PM), Omar (CTO)

Summary: demo of prompt-sets, regression alerting, AB comparisons in Redwood Console + Optimize. Walkthrough included traffic split config and how to wire alerts back to PagerDuty/slack and to their telemetry stack. Discussed hosted vs private options, SOC2, KMS, and expected pilot scope.

Topics: prompt set design, regression hypothesis, traffic splits, evaluation metrics (BLEU/EM/semantic match), latency vs cost tradeoffs, private deployment constraints.

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Sofia from Redwood, AE on the account, with Marcus our Solutions Eng. Quick round of intros?
[00:10] Elaine: Hi all, Elaine, Head of ML at Mariner. We're exploring automated quality monitoring for our logistics assistant - reduce hallucinations on ETAs and bill-of-lading summaries.
[00:18] Ben: Ben, product. Mostly focused on UX impact and what a pilot would look like.
[00:22] Omar: Omar, CTO, will be looking at security and deployment options.
[00:27] Marcus: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: prompt set bakeoff demo in Console + Optimize; show regression alerting & AB compare; then cover infra/security. Feel free to interrupt.

[00:37] Sofia: Couple housekeeping items — we'll share the deck and a benchmark spreadsheet after. Link in chat: https://redwood.ai/decks/prompt-bakeoff (note: demo recording + sample notebook).

[01:05] Marcus: Alright jumping in — first screen is the Prompt Sets page. You can create named prompt sets, upload CSVs of prompts, and tag expected outputs or scoring functions. For Mariner you might have sets like "ETA clamshells" or "BOL_summary" — sorry, "BOL" stands for bill of lading.
[01:30] Marcus: We're going to run a bakeoff across three model variants: hosted open-weights small, hosted q4_bert-ish — laughable name here — and a private dedicated large. The Compare tab will show token costs, latency distribution, and quality metrics side-by-side.
[01:52] Ben: Quick question — are the metrics customizable? We need to score on domain-specific criteria, e.g., numeric-correctness and carrier-code-matching.
[01:58] Marcus: Yep, you can plug in custom metric functions. We shipped a JS/Python evaluator; you can also send outputs to your existing eval pipeline via webhook. Example in the notebook.

[02:20] Marcus: Starting a run now... you'll see the run queued, then it goes through traffic split or pure batch mode. For live A/B we can route 10% to model A and 90% to baseline, or do time-based splits.
[02:40] Elaine: We're really sensitive to latency on the mobile tracking widget — anything above 400ms is bad. How do you control that?
[02:47] Marcus: We have latency SLO routing — you can pin fast variants for low-seq paths and let cheaper variants handle longer flows. Also automatic KV cache — sometimes shows up as "KV cash" in older transcribes — that saves repeated prefix tokens.

[03:10] Sofia: To address security quickly: we support SSO/SAML, SCIM, RBAC, and KMS integration. For Private deployments we offer a VPC option and on-prem appliance.
[03:22] Omar: On KMS — is HSM supported or only cloud KMS? We need to keep keys in our HSM for regulatory reasons.
[03:28] Marcus: HSM integrations are supported via our customer-managed KMS layer; we can work through specifics in the pilot. We'll include that in the security pack.

[03:50] Marcus: Back to the console. Here's an AB compare view — top shows distribution of semantic similarity scores, middle shows token costs per thousand, bottom shows latency percentiles. The UI flags regressions automatically using the baseline you'd choose.
[04:10] Ben: How are regressions detected? Is it purely statistical drift or model-output-based?
[04:16] Marcus: It's a hybrid. We run hypothesis-based checks on your prompt sets and compute metrics; statistically significant drops trigger alerts. You can tune alert thresholds or have a gradual sensitivity ramp to avoid alert fatigue.

[04:38] Sofia: For your team, we'd recommend starting with conservative thresholds so you get signal but not noise. You can incrementally tighten after a couple weeks.

[05:00] Elaine: Can we map alerts to specific user journeys? Like if a pickup ETA falls outside bounds, open a ticket with the trace id?
[05:07] Marcus: Yes — alerts include context (prompt id, sample input, metadata, model variant, trace id). You can route to Slack, PagerDuty, or send to your own Kafka stream.

[05:30] Ben: Do you keep the raw model outputs in Redwood logs? We have retention policies.
[05:36] Marcus: By default, hosted keeps minimal logs for debugging; you control retention. In Private deployments you can retain everything locally; we can adapt to Mariner retention needs.

[06:00] Omar: Quick procurement question — if we choose Dedicated, what's the commitment model? We might prefer reserved capacity to avoid noisy neighbors.
[06:07] Sofia: Dedicated is commit-based monthly/annual. We can map predicted throughput to a reserved pool. For pilots we often recommend a short trial with burst credits.

[06:30] Marcus: Running the bakeoff completed — summary table popping up. Model B shows slightly higher semantic score but 30% higher tail latency. You can click into examples to inspect where scoring disagrees.

[06:52] Marcus: Example 1 — baseline summarizes shipment line items correctly, Model B added an extra carrier name (hallucination). The pairwise compare view lets you mark which output is preferred and store that as a labeled example.
[07:15] Elaine: Is there a way to do pairwise labeling at scale with our ops team? That manual step could be big.
[07:20] Marcus: We integrate with labeling partners and also provide a lightweight UI for your ops folks to do batch pairwise reviews. You can prioritize examples that triggered regressions.

[07:45] Ben: About cost — when you show token cost, is that counting both input+output? We need accurate forecasting.
[07:52] Marcus: Yes both. The cost model in the console is configurable to your pricing plan. For Dedicated you get flat-rate capacity; for Hosted it's per-token. We also show projected monthly burn based on traffic.

[08:15] Sofia: One nuance — sometimes customers conflate token cost with infra cost; our Optimize tooling will recommend batching/quantization profiles to save unit cost while keeping quality.

[08:40] Marcus: Now demoing alert flow — I set a regression threshold on the semantic score; when a batch violates it, the system creates an incident and runs a small triage: it surfaces examples, the diff view, and a suggested action: rollback to previous variant or open remediation label task.

[09:05] Elaine: If the alert says rollback, is that automatic?
[09:08] Marcus: It can be automatic or manual — you configure the policy. For high-risk, customers prefer manual canary removal; for low-risk you can auto-fallback to a safe variant.

[09:30] Ben: For the A/B traffic split, can we do dynamic splitting based on model confidence?
[09:36] Marcus: Yes — you can weight by model-provided confidence or use heuristics. We also support user-weighted splits (sticky buckets) so a single user sees consistent variant.

[10:00] Sofia: We're getting a few questions in chat about integrations: Datadog, Splunk, and S3 for artifacts. All supported — we export eval telemetry and artifact bundles.

[10:18] Marcus: Switching to a quick private deployment note — for VPC/on-prem we provide a control plane that you can host; the inference layer runs in your network. There are a couple of tradeoffs: you manage infra but get full data residency.

[10:40] Omar: Latency guarantee in Private—do you provide the same optimized kernels? We run on A100s and some older T4s.
[10:47] Marcus: The runtime compiles kernels to hardware and we adapt to available GPUs. For older hardware we might recommend quantized profiles; we can run a short compatibility benchmark during the pilot.

[11:10] Elaine: A practical concern — how do we seed the prompt sets? We have a big mix of user utterances and structured forms.
[11:16] Marcus: You can import logs in CSV, map fields, and define extraction helpers. We also offer wrangling scripts in the notebook. Start with a few hundred representative examples per intent.

[11:40] Ben: On evaluation metrics, we saw BLEU referenced in the docs — can we adopt semantic metrics instead? BLEU isn't great for our paraphrase tolerance.
[11:47] Marcus: Absolutely — you can choose embedding-based similarity, token overlap, or custom rule-based validators. The Compare UI will let you pick the metric set for the bakeoff.

[12:10] Marcus: Now I'll show the regression alert history — you can see incidents over time, drill into the cause, and see which model rollout correlated with the metric drop. There's an auto-correlation helper that sometimes mislabels variables but it's useful.

[12:40] Sofia: One thing we've seen is customers want to tie regressions to PRs or model deploys. We support linking to GitHub or your CI so you can trace a regression to a build.

[13:00] Ben: That would be huge for our SRE workflows.

[13:08] Marcus: Quick demo of scoring functions — here's a numeric-check that ensures ETAs are within 5 minutes of ground truth. We can run these offline as regression tests in a nightly job.

[13:30] Elaine: Would that be part of the pilot? We want nightly regression alerts for core intents.
[13:35] Sofia: Yes, pilot can include nightly runs and daily dashboards. We'll scope what gets monitored initially.

[13:50] Marcus: Example of pairwise A/B: you can mark A preferred, B preferred, or tie. Those labels feed into model selection and we can auto-promote winning variants.

[14:10] Omar: Who owns the model variants if we do private? Do we host them or do you host them?
[14:16] Marcus: In Private you host the inference layer and you control the model binaries. For Dedicated we can host the model but in an isolated pool. For Hosted we manage everything.

[14:36] Ben: How easy is it to roll back a change that caused a regression?
[14:40] Marcus: One click rollback to previous model pinned, or auto fallback to a canary you define.

[15:00] Sofia: Quick note on auditability — every evaluation, label, and alert has an audit trail and is exportable for compliance.

[15:15] Elaine: Great. On privacy, we need PII scrubbing in logs to meet GDPR. Does Redwood scrub PII automatically?
[15:22] Marcus: We provide built-in PII scrubbing templates; you can augment with your own rules and it runs before artifacts leave your network for Private deployments. For Hosted, you can set scrubbing policies.

[15:45] Ben: Back to the bakeoff output — we want to know if a metric drop is due to distribution shift or model regression. Does the tooling help separate those?

[15:53] Marcus: Yes, we show covariate shift detection, sample-level diffs, and can run per-intent breakdowns. Sometimes the UI mislabels columns (transcription artifact) but it's there.

[16:20] Sofia: Example customer story: one retail customer caught a pricing hallucination via automatic regression alert and rolled back in under 20 minutes.

[16:35] Elaine: Ok, what's the minimum data we need for a pilot?

[16:39] Marcus: For meaningful results, ~2k labeled/representative prompts across core intents, and logs for an initial week to calibrate thresholds. We'll work with your data team to extract and sanitize.

[16:58] Ben: Is there a way to simulate load for the pilot to test latency?

[17:04] Marcus: Yes — we provide a simple load harness that runs generated traffic with the same distribution; we also include a stress script to measure P95/P99.

[17:28] Omar: On contract terms — does pilot incur cost? We want a short smoke with minimal commitment.

[17:33] Sofia: Usually pilot costs are modest and can be credited against a committed Dedicated contract. We'll include options in the SOW.

[17:50] Marcus: Demo wrap-up — key takeaways: you can run prompt-set bakeoffs, tune custom metrics, configure regression alerts, and run AB/traffic splits. Pilot recommended scope: 2k prompts, nightly regression checks, and a small dedicated capacity or Private eval lane.

[18:20] Elaine: A couple of nitty-gritty items — can we get the raw evaluation logs streamed to our event hub (Kafka)?
[18:25] Marcus: Yes, Kafka sink supported. We'll send sample connector configs.

[18:40] Ben: And the eval notebook - can it be run in our CI?
[18:44] Marcus: Yep, it's a lightweight Python script that uses the Redwood eval SDK. I'll share repo link.

[19:05] Sofia: I'm going to recap next steps in chat. Action items in the notes.

[19:15] Ben: One more question — how do you handle shadowing traffic (send to Redwood but not impact production)?
[19:21] Marcus: Shadowing supported; we can mirror production traffic into a safe lane for evaluation, never returning results to the user. Useful for looking for regressions pre-rollout.

[19:45] Elaine: Any limitations on the size of prompt sets? We have thousands of historical queries.
[19:50] Marcus: Console can handle large sets; for very large corpuses we recommend sampling and prioritizing by signal. Storage of artifacts is configurable.

[20:10] Omar: From a security POV, we'll need the SOC2 report and pen test summary.

[20:16] Sofia: We'll attach our SOC2 report and a redacted pen test overview in the follow-up.

[20:30] Marcus: Quick demo of regression alert email: shows top failing prompts and suggested rollback. You can drill into the pairwise view to accept or reject.

[20:50] Ben: Could we wire alerts into our internal ticketing to auto-open a JIRA with linked examples?

[20:55] Marcus: Yes, JIRA integration in the integrations panel.

[21:10] Sofia: Wrapping toward pilot scope — one option: Hosted pilot with 30-day eval, nightly regression checks, and 10% traffic shadowing. Alternate: Private trial in your VPC limited to a week for compatibility testing.

[21:35] Elaine: I like the private compatibility run first to verify kernels and latency on our hosts.

[21:42] Omar: Agreed — after that, we'll decide whether to move to Dedicated or keep Private.

[22:00] Sofia: Great. I'll send SOW options. Marcus will share the runbook and notebook. Can we confirm the date to receive sample prompts?

[22:10] Elaine: I'll aim for 2026-09-20 to deliver the 2k sanitized samples.

[22:18] Ben: We'll review SOW with procurement; Omar will loop in legal for data residency clauses.

[22:25] Marcus: Last note — we recommend enabling a low-sensitivity regression check for the first 2 weeks, then tune. It reduces noise while you calibrate.

[22:40] Sofia: Okay folks, thanks for the time. Any final quick questions?

[22:45] Elaine: Nothing else. Thank you, useful walkthrough.
[22:48] Ben: Thanks y'all.
[22:50] Omar: Thanks.

[22:55] Sofia: Bye everyone. We'll follow up with materials and next steps.

End of transcript.
